extracted.intended_audience: early-18th-century readers of The Spectator; educated public interested in manners, literature, and social critique
extracted.subtask_description: Selections from The Spectator (Addison & Steele) discussing marriage, conjugal love, public behaviour, a deputation for observing manners, and rules of precedence in the learned/ theatrical world. The page mixes moral prescription, reportage-instruction, and satirical social-ranking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjugal love is a higher refinement than amour with a mistress
rubrics_metrics.description: “If Love be any Refinement, Conjugal Love must be certainly so in a much higher Degree.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conjugal love is described as a ‘regular and uniform Endeavour to make your self valuable…to one whom you have chosen to be the Companion of your Life.’ It cultivates the mind, is the parent of substantial virtues and agreeable qualities, and is compared to the vital heat, whereas passion for a mistress resembles the flame of a fever.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters from good-natured husbands to wives should be simple and sincere
rubrics_metrics.description: “Friendship, Tenderness and Constancy, drest in a Simplicity of Expression, recommend themselves by a more native Elegance, than passionate Raptures, extravagant Encomiums, and slavish Adoration.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare epistolary styles: letters of a husband (good-nature) to his wife have an inherent elegance through simplicity and constancy; letters from gallants to mistresses, though perhaps florid, often induce nausea when read together. The passage uses the imagined cabinet of Narcissa to show the superiority of domestic, sincere correspondence.

rubrics_metrics.name: The model husband (Benevolus) displays public esteem and private felicity
rubrics_metrics.description: “Benevolus…appears to have every good Quality and desirable Ornament. Abroad he is reverenced and esteemed; at home beloved and happy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ideal husband’s domestic happiness radiates outward: habitual complacency ‘shines in his Countenance, enlivens his Wit, and seasons his Conversation.’ His private virtues make him a steadfast friend and agreeable companion in public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectator-deputy general remit to observe public manners (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorization of Mr. John Sly: to keep a strict eye upon all persons and things conveyed in coaches, carts, or on foot between London and Westminster from nine in the morning till four in the afternoon, and to report observations to the Spectator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a procedural rubric: the deputy must not depart from his observatory, must observe behaviour of all classes of travellers, and send ‘the speediest Advice’ when offences occur. The remit includes many specific reporting points (see related, more specific metrics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe neglect or affectation toward former acquaintances after rising in station
rubrics_metrics.description: “Observe the Behaviour of all Persons…what Notice they take of their Foot-Acquaintance, and send me the speediest Advice, when they are guilty of overlooking, turning from, or appearing grave and distant to their old Friends.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report instances where people newly seated in coaches or elevated in rank slight or shun previous acquaintances; such behaviour is singled out as a social offence to be ‘nipp’d in the bud.’

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess public comportment of married couples (appearance of fondness vs coldness)
rubrics_metrics.description: “When Man and Wife are in the same Coach, you are to see whether they appear pleased or tired with each other, and whether they carry the due Mein in the Eye of the World between Fondness and Coldness.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The deputy should note whether spouses display appropriate demeanour publicly—neither excessive display nor offhand coldness—and report deviations as indicative of domestic disorder or triumph of affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report whether persons preserve their former countenance after gaining honour or riches
rubrics_metrics.description: “You are carefully to behold all such as shall have Addition of Honour or Riches, and Report whether they preserve the Countenance they had before such Addition.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion judges constancy of character after advancement: observe if elevation alters behaviour, affectation, or airs; preservation of former demeanour is implicitly praised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess persons on foot for appropriate demeanour and dress; identify discretion by footwear
rubrics_metrics.description: “As to Persons on Foot, you are to be attentive whether they are pleased with their Condition, and are dress'd suitable to it; but especially to distinguish such as appear discreet, by a low-heel Shoe, with the decent Ornament of a Leather-Garter.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether pedestrians comport themselves and dress suitably to their station; specific sartorial signals (low-heel shoe, leather garter) are given as signs of discretion to be recorded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record country gentlemen who have abandoned hunting for military fashion
rubrics_metrics.description: “To write down the Name of such Country Gentlemen as, upon the Approach of Peace, have left the Hunting for the Military Cock of the Hat.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note ostentatious changes in habit or fashion among rural gentry (e.g., adopting military dress over traditional pursuits) as a social marker worth reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record boorish public behaviour (strutting, noise, swearing at drivers)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Of all who strut, make a Noise, and swear at the Drivers of Coaches to make haste, when they see it impossible they should pass.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document vulgar or aggressive conduct in the street—posturing, peevish shouting, and abusive language toward coachmen—as examples of manners needing correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record pretentious young gentlemen in coach-boxes striving at affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: “Of all young Gentlemen in Coach-boxes, who labour at a Perfection in what they are sure to be excelled by the meanest of the People.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note ostentatious affectations among youthful elite who display exaggerated airs or skills in public—especially when they will plainly be outdone—marking them for admonition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforce that coaches and passengers give way according to course of business (traffic order)
rubrics_metrics.description: “You are to do all that in you lies that Coaches and Passengers give way according to the Course of Business, all the Morning in Term-Time towards Westminster, the rest of the Year towards the Exchange.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The deputy should promote orderly traffic flow by ensuring customary right-of-way patterns are observed depending on season and business hours; this is presented as a civic-manners duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors ranked by book format (folio > quarto > octavo etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Author of a Folio…sets himself above the Author of a Quarto; the Author of a Quarto above the Author of an Octavo; and so on…to an Author in Twenty Fours.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A satirical ‘table of laws’ for precedence in the learned world: physical format and size of one’s publication are treated as the basis for social ranking among authors; examples of seating and deference illustrate the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printers and booksellers take precedence according to the merits of the authors they represent
rubrics_metrics.description: “All Printers and Booksellers take the Wall of one another, according to the abovementioned Merits of the Authors to whom they respectively belong.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers’ social position follows the perceived rank of their authors: the commercial agents inherit status from their authors’ place in the format-based hierarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage precedence rules: tragedian above comedian; tragi-comedy between; queens/heroines rank above comic performers
rubrics_metrics.description: “Among [actors] it is a standing and uncontroverted Principle, that a Tragedian always takes place of a Comedian…The same Distinction is observed among the Ladies of the Theatre. Queens and Heroines preserve their Rank…while those who are Waiting-Women and Maids of Honour upon the Stage, keep their Distance also behind the Scenes.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A theatrical hierarchy is prescribed: serious dramatic performers (tragedians, heroics) claim precedence in social situations over comic actors and burlesque writers; tragi-comic authors take an intermediate place. The maxim ‘Once a King, and always a King’ underscores permanent rank.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour should not invert the value of sobriety and good-nature
rubrics_metrics.description: “I am apt to think it was about the same Time, that Good-Nature…came first to be render'd suspicious, and in danger of being transferred from its original Sense to so distant an Idea as that of Folly…It has been my Ambition…to restore…the proper Ideas of things.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prescriptive standard for taste and satire: avoid treating sobriety as spiritlessness or good-nature as folly. The writer claims a corrective aim—to restore proper ideas and resist fashions of wit that make civic virtues objects of ridicule.
